stops.title: The First World War
stops.blurb: On 28 June 1914 the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was assassinated in Sarajevo. By August the Allies, among them Britain, France and Russia, were at war with the Central Powers, Germany and Austria-Hungary. Fighting spread to Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and stopped on 11 November 1918. More than 8.5 million soldiers died, and as many as 13 million civilians.
stops.dateNote: No official body kept count of civilian deaths; the figure is an estimate by historians.

stops.title: Revolution in Russia, depression everywhere
stops.blurb: In 1917 two revolutions shook Russia. The first overthrew the tsar's government and the second brought the Bolsheviks to power; civil war followed until 1922. In August 1929 an economic slump began in the United States and spread around the globe. In Germany it brought mass unemployment and weakened the young republic. In January 1933 Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party came to power.
stops.dateNote: The Depression hit bottom in the United States in March 1933 and dragged on through the 1930s; full recovery came only during the Second World War.

stops.title: From two billion people to eight
stops.blurb: Around 1927 there were two billion people alive. By 1974 there were four billion, and in 2022 the count passed eight billion. The two world wars barely show on the curve. Growth was fastest in the 1960s, at over 2 percent a year. It has slowed since, to under 1 percent a year today.

stops.title: The Second World War and the Holocaust
stops.blurb: Japan had been at war with China since 1937. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and in December 1941 Japan attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor. Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan on 2 September. Some 55 to 65 million people died, most of them civilians. Six million were Jews, murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators in the Holocaust.
stops.dateNote: Totals for the war's dead are estimates: the museums cited here give 55 million and over 65 million.

stops.title: The atomic bomb and the Cold War
stops.blurb: On 16 July 1945 the United States exploded the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In August it dropped two on Japan, killing 90,000 to 166,000 people in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki within four months. The Soviet Union tested its own in 1949. In their long rivalry, the Cold War, the world's stockpile passed 60,000 warheads by 1986. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
stops.dateNote: The number killed by the two bombs is not known precisely: records were destroyed and whole families died.

links.label: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

stops.title: Empires end
stops.blurb: The United Nations began on 24 October 1945 with 51 member states. At that time some 750 million people, nearly a third of humanity, lived in territories ruled by colonial powers. In 1947 British India was divided into India and Pakistan, with great loss of life. By 1960 three dozen new states in Asia and Africa had won independence. The UN now has 193 members.
stops.dateNote: Decolonisation went on after 1960: the UN counts 80 former colonies that have gained independence since 1945.

stops.title: China: revolution, famine and reform
stops.blurb: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong declared the People's Republic of China, ending a long civil war. His Great Leap Forward, a drive to industrialise within a few years, forced peasants into communes and into making steel. Harvests collapsed, and between 1959 and 1961 some 30 million people starved. In 1979, less than three years after Mao's death, reformers dissolved the communes and freed farm prices.
stops.debate: Estimates of deaths in the famine run from about 30 million to 45 million. The precise number will never be known.

stops.title: Lives that last decades longer
stops.blurb: A baby born in 1950 could expect, on the world average, to live about 46 years. By 2023 that had risen to 73. Every region gained: Africa went from 37 years to 64, Asia from 42 to 75, and Europe from 62 to 79. The gap between regions narrowed but did not close. The dip in 2020 and 2021 is the COVID-19 pandemic.

links.label: Life expectancy, Our World in Data

chart.title: Life expectancy at birth, 1950 to 2023
chart.note: Life expectancy at birth is an average. Much of the rise comes from fewer children dying young, not only from adults living longer.

stops.title: Carbon dioxide: the cost of cheap energy
stops.blurb: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the air. In 1850 the world released about 0.2 billion tonnes a year. By 1950 it was about 6 billion, and in 2024 about 39 billion. Nearly nine-tenths of everything released since 1750 has come since 1950, and more than half since 1990.

stops.title: Into space
stops.blurb: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite: a sphere the size of a beach ball that circled Earth about every 98 minutes. In April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, on a flight of 108 minutes. On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of Apollo 11 walked on the Moon, watched by an estimated 650 million people.

stops.title: The web, and a world online
stops.blurb: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, working at the CERN laboratory in Geneva, proposed a way to link documents across computer networks. By the end of 1990 the first web server and browser were running, and by October 1993 there were over 200 servers. In 2005 about 16 percent of the world's people used the internet. By 2019 it was more than half, and in 2025 about 74 percent.

links.label: History of the World Wide Web

chart.title: Share of people using the internet, 2005 to 2025
chart.note: World totals begin in 2005. A user is anyone who went online in the last three months.

stops.title: Fewer in extreme poverty, more who can read
stops.blurb: In 1990, 43 percent of the world's people lived in extreme poverty, which the World Bank defines as less than 3 dollars a day. By 2024 it was about 10 percent, though the pandemic year of 2020 pushed the share up. Reading spread too. About 12 percent of people could read and write in 1820; today more than four in five can.

chart.title: Share of people in extreme poverty, 1990 to 2024
chart.note: Extreme poverty here means living on less than $3 a day, in 2021 prices adjusted for the cost of living in each country.

stops.title: A world of cities
stops.blurb: In 1950 about 29 percent of the world's people lived in towns and cities, going by each country's own definition of urban. In 2007 the share passed half for the first time, and by 2025 it was about 58 percent. The date depends on the definition. Measured by one shared standard that counts towns with cities, most people have lived in urban areas since at least the 1950s.

chart.title: Share of people living in towns and cities, 1950 to 2025
chart.note: United Nations figures, using each country's own definition of an urban area.

stops.title: Eight billion
stops.blurb: The United Nations marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world's population reached eight billion. It had taken 12 years to grow from seven billion, and the next billion is expected to take about 15, because growth is slowing. Our species is about 300,000 years old. On the time strip on this story's first page, nearly all of that growth sits in the last thin sliver.
stops.dateNote: The date is a projection: no one can count the world's people to the day.

p: Both sides expected a quick victory. Instead the war in western Europe settled into trenches: a line of ditches and fortifications that at its longest ran some 475 miles (about 760 kilometres), roughly from the North Sea to the Swiss border. Long-range artillery, poison gas, tanks and aircraft killed on a new scale, and commanders were slow to change their tactics. On 1 July 1916, the first day of the battle of the Somme, the British Army alone suffered over 57,000 casualties.

In 1917 Russia had two revolutions and left the war, and the United States joined it. Germany asked for an armistice, an agreement to stop fighting, and the guns on the western front fell silent at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

By then a second disaster was under way. A new influenza spread around the world in three waves within about a year. The first, in the spring of 1918, made many people ill but killed few. The second, from September to November 1918, was highly fatal, and a third followed early in 1919. About a third of the world's people, some 500 million, fell ill.
Armies recorded their dead, so military losses are known fairly well: Germany lost about 1.77 million soldiers and Russia about 1.7 million. No official agency kept careful count of civilians.

Influenza was not a disease that doctors had to report in 1918, so its toll is rebuilt from death records, which are missing for much of the world. The virus itself was unknown at the time. In 1995 a team began reading its genetic code from autopsy tissue kept since the autumn of 1918. That work showed the virus was the ancestor of almost every influenza A virus that has circulated in people since.

The number of influenza deaths is still argued over. A calculation in the 1920s put it near 21.5 million. A 1991 study raised that to between 24.7 and 39.3 million, and a 2002 study to about 50 million, adding that the true figure might be twice as high. In 2018 another team, using death records from 13 countries and British India, estimated 17.4 million and judged totals above 25 million unrealistic.

Where the pandemic began is not known: the records are too thin to say. Nor is it settled why this influenza, unlike any before or since, killed so many healthy adults between about 20 and 40 years old.
The war brought down the German emperor and the Russian tsar, and the harsh peace terms that followed fed the resentment on which the Nazi movement later grew.

By every estimate above, the pandemic killed more people in about a year than died as soldiers in four years of war. Descendants of the 1918 virus still circulate, and it remains a warning for public health.

Plants need nitrogen in a form their roots can take up, and for all of history farmers had only what soils and a few crops such as peas and beans supplied. That set a ceiling on harvests. In 1908 the German chemist Fritz Haber found a way to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia, which plants can use. Another German chemist, Carl Bosch, scaled the process up for industry, and factory-made fertiliser went on sale from 1910.

The second change was in the plants themselves. From the 1960s, publicly funded breeders produced high-yielding varieties of wheat, rice and maize and adapted them to the tropics, a campaign known as the Green Revolution. Between 1960 and 2000, yields in developing countries rose by 208 percent for wheat, 109 percent for rice and 157 percent for maize.
Over about fifty years the population of the developing world more than doubled, and its cereal harvest tripled, from only 30 percent more farmland.

Nobody can count the people fed by fertiliser directly. Researchers work it out from nitrogen budgets: how much of the nitrogen in crops, and so in the protein people eat, came from factories. One widely used estimate, published in 2008, is that synthetic fertiliser supported 42 percent of all births in the century after its invention, and fed 44 percent of the world's people in 2000. A separate study put the share at about half in 2019.

For the Green Revolution, economists compare what happened with models of a world without the new varieties. One such estimate is that food production in developing countries would have been almost 20 percent lower.
The estimates agree on a range, 40 to 50 percent of humanity, more than on a number. Fertiliser arrived together with better seed, irrigation and machines, and separating their effects is hard.

The Green Revolution's costs are also argued over. Heavy use of water, fertiliser and pesticides degraded soils and polluted water beyond the fields. The new seeds worked best on good, well-watered land, so poorer and drier regions were left behind. In sub-Saharan Africa, varieties brought from Asia and Latin America suited local conditions badly, and suitable ones came only in the 1980s.

In the 18th century Thomas Malthus argued that population would always outrun food, and in the 1960s famine on a vast scale was widely predicted. It did not happen. The world went from about 1.65 billion people in 1900 to more than 8 billion, and roughly every second person alive today is fed by nitrogen taken from the air.
Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party came to power in Germany in January 1933. Hatred of Jews was at the root of their beliefs, and they began to persecute Germany's Jews at once.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war two days later. By 1942 Germany and its allies controlled most of Europe. In June 1941 they invaded the Soviet Union. German units began mass shootings of Jewish men, and soon of whole communities, on the edges of towns across eastern Europe. As many as two million Jews were murdered in shootings or in vans that used poison gas.

From late 1941 Nazi Germany built five killing centres in occupied Poland for the sole purpose of murdering Jews with poison gas: Chełmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau. Jews from across Europe were deported to them by train. About 2.7 million Jews were murdered there, about a million of them at Auschwitz.

At Stalingrad a German army surrendered to Soviet forces in February 1943, and from then on Germany was pushed back. It surrendered in May 1945. Japan surrendered on 2 September 1945, after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

As they began to lose, the Nazis tried to destroy the evidence, digging up mass graves and burning records. They did not succeed. German documents survived in great numbers and were used in the trials of Nazi leaders after the war, alongside the accounts of survivors and witnesses.

The figure of six million comes from two kinds of evidence: German records of deportations and killings, and comparisons of census counts of Jewish communities before and after the war. Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, has gathered the names of more than 4.7 million of the victims.
The number cannot be exact. Serious studies give totals between five and six million: early calculations ranged from 5.1 million to 5.95 million, and later ones from 5.29 million to six million.

The Nazis and their allies also murdered millions of other people, among them around 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war, around 1.8 million non-Jewish Poles, 250,000 to 500,000 Roma, and 250,000 to 300,000 people with disabilities.
Totals for all deaths in the war are rougher still. The museums cited here give 55 million and over 65 million.

No war has killed more people, and most of the dead were civilians. The Holocaust was an attempt by a modern state to murder an entire people, carried out with railways, record-keeping and purpose-built killing centres.
What came next was shaped by it. The United Nations was formed in 1945 to prevent another such war, and political and military leaders of the defeated powers were put on trial for war crimes.

For most of human existence, infectious diseases were the leading causes of illness and death. In 1910 the German scientist Paul Ehrlich brought out Salvarsan, a drug for syphilis found by testing hundreds of chemicals one after another. In the 1930s came the sulfa drugs. On 3 September 1928 Alexander Fleming had noticed that a mould, *Penicillium*, killed bacteria, but he could not purify its active substance. In 1940 a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain did, and by 1945 penicillin was being mass-produced. Most kinds of antibiotic in use today were discovered between the 1950s and the 1970s.

Vaccines reached far more people too. Smallpox had killed up to 30 percent of those who caught it, for at least 3,000 years. In 1967 the World Health Organization began an intensified campaign of vaccination and of tracking down cases. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the WHO declared the disease eradicated. In 1974 it had launched a programme to bring vaccines against other diseases to children everywhere.

The chart's figures come from United Nations estimates built on censuses, death registers and surveys. The effect of vaccines is harder to see, because it is a count of deaths that did not happen. A 2024 study used models of 14 diseases to compare the real world with one where no one had been vaccinated since 1974. It estimated that vaccination averted 154 million deaths in fifty years, 146 million of them among children under five.

How much of the gain is owed to medicine is a real question. The same study credits vaccination with 40 percent of the fall in infant deaths since 1974, which leaves most of the fall to other causes. The United Nations lists public health, nutrition and personal hygiene alongside medicine. Because the figure for deaths averted comes from models, it depends on their assumptions.
Antibiotics carry a risk of their own. Bacteria evolve resistance to them, as Fleming himself warned, and no new class of antibiotic has been discovered since the 1970s.

Smallpox is the only human infectious disease ever wiped out. Since 1974 children's chances of surviving have improved in every region of the world, and that is a large part of what lifted the world's average length of life from 46 years in 1950 to 73.
